abstract: Barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) is among the world’s earliest domesticated and most important crop plants. It is diploid with a large haploid genome of 5.1 gigabases (Gb). Here we present an integrated and ordered physical, genetic and functional sequence resource that describes the barley gene-space in a structured whole-genome context. We developed a physical map of 4.98 Gb, with more than 3.90 Gb anchored to a high-resolution genetic map. Projecting a deep whole-genome shotgun assembly, complementary DNA and deep RNA sequence data onto this framework supports 79,379 transcript clusters, including 26,159 ‘high-confidence’ genes with homology support from other plant genomes. Abundant alternative splicing, premature termination codons and novel transcriptionally active regions suggest that post-transcriptional processing forms an important regulatory layer. Survey sequences from diverse accessions reveal a landscape of extensive single-nucleotide variation. Our data provide a platform for both genome-assisted research and enabling contemporary crop improvement. An integrated high-resolution genetic, physical and shotgun sequence assembly of the barley genome, one of the earliest domesticated and most important crops, is described; it will provide a platform for genome-assisted research and future crop improvement. Two groups in this issue report the compilation and analysis of the genome sequences of major cereal crops — bread wheat and barley — providing important resources for future crop improvement. Bread wheat accounts for one-fifth of the calories consumed by humankind. It has a very large and complex hexaploid genome of 17 Gigabases. Michael Bevan and colleagues have analysed the genome using 454 pyrosequencing and compared it with diploid ancestral and progenitor genomes. The authors discovered significant loss of gene family members upon polyploidization and domestication, and expansion of gene classes that may be associated with crop productivity. Barley is one of the earliest domesticated plant crops. Although diploid, it has a very large genome of 5.1 Gigabases. Nils Stein and colleagues describe a physical map anchored to a high-resolution genetic map, on top of which they have overlaid a deep whole-genome shotgun assembly, cDNA and RNA-seq data to provide the first in-depth genome-wide survey of the barley genome.

narrative:
Short impact summary

A physical, genetic and functional sequence assembly of the barley genome (2012) in Nature. 1513 citations.

Full narrative

A physical, genetic and functional sequence assembly of the barley genome (2012) in Nature is authored by Klaus Mayer, Thomas Nussbaumer and Heidrun Gundlach. Topics: Sequence (biology), Genome, Biology, Computational biology and Whole genome sequencing.

1513 citations (OpenAlex). Citations peaked in 2015 with 174 citing works. Citing venues include Frontiers in Plant Science, PLoS ONE and bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory).

It is discussed on Wikipedia (3 mentions). 3 online mentions.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This Nature article has had substantial scholarly impact, with 1,513 OpenAlex citations and a top 1% field- and year-normalized citation standing. Its influence is also visible in downstream reuse across the research record, where it is documented as being reused in more than 1,500 works, especially in plant genetics, genomics, and barley-focused research. The article’s reach extends beyond citations into instructional and public reference contexts, including Wikipedia and a recorded YouTube explanation.

Full narrative

A physical, genetic and functional sequence assembly of the barley genome quickly became a foundational resource for barley genomics. The article presents an integrated whole-genome framework for barley gene space, combining physical mapping, genetic anchoring, and functional sequence information to place a large and complex crop genome into an ordered context. That methodological and resource-building contribution helps explain why the paper has remained highly visible in the literature more than a decade after publication.

The citation record shows sustained and broad scholarly uptake. OpenAlex reports 1,513 citations, and the work falls in the top 1% of its field and year. The citing literature is concentrated in plant science and genetics venues, with especially strong presence in journals such as Frontiers in Plant Science, PLoS ONE, BMC Genomics, Theoretical and Applied Genetics, and The Plant Journal. The subject profile of citing works centers on wheat and barley genetics, genetic mapping, chromosomal variation, disease resistance, and genomics, indicating that the assembly has served as a reference point for both basic and applied crop science.

The downstream reuse graph further reinforces this picture of durable infrastructure. The article is documented as reused by 1,529 works spanning articles, book chapters, preprints, reviews, dissertations, datasets, and other scholarly outputs. Recent citing studies continue to draw on it in current barley research, including work on haplotype-based mapping, pangenome approaches, transcriptomic responses, disease resistance, and breeding-related analyses. This pattern suggests that the paper is not only historically important but remains part of the live technical base for barley genomics.

Other indicators point to a wider but more modest public and pedagogical footprint. Scite records 946 citation statements, with supportive mentions present in the citation discourse. Wikipedia references appear on pages related to barley, plant genome sequencing, and a scientist profile, and there is also a recorded educational video that explicitly links to the paper. These signals do not replace the citation record, but they show that the article has also become part of broader explanatory and teaching materials around crop genomics.

The article’s production and stewardship context also fits a large collaborative genomics project. It was supported by Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council funding, and the author list reflects a multi-institution effort spanning major plant genomics centers and research universities. Taken together, the record shows a landmark genome-resource paper whose main impact lies in enabling subsequent barley genetics, breeding, and genomics research, with continuing visibility in both specialist and educational contexts.
